questions.stem_markdown: A 2-year-old boy is found to have iron deficiency anaemia. His parents report he drinks about 2 L of cow’s milk each day and otherwise eats poorly. What is the best management?

options.text: Blood transfusion and no dietary change
Oral iron supplements and reduce cow’s milk intake to less than 400 mL/day
Oral iron supplements and reduce cow’s milk intake to less than 1 L/day
Stop milk completely and start intravenous iron
Reassure and repeat blood tests in 3 months

questions.explanation_markdown: The source material links excessive cow’s milk intake in toddlers with iron deficiency anaemia and specifically supports treatment with oral iron plus marked reduction of cow’s milk intake, with <400 mL/day being the best option offered. Excess cow’s milk contributes through low iron content, reduced iron absorption, and occult gastrointestinal blood loss.

why_others_wrong.A: Transfusion is not the routine first-line response to dietary iron deficiency in a stable toddler.
why_others_wrong.C: This is better than no change, but the source set specifically supports reducing intake further to <400 mL/day.
why_others_wrong.D: The source material supports oral iron and dietary correction, not immediate intravenous iron or complete milk exclusion.
why_others_wrong.E: Observation alone leaves the underlying cause untreated.

key_takeaways: Excess cow’s milk intake is a classic cause of toddler iron deficiency anaemia.
Management should address both iron replacement and diet.
A major reduction in milk intake is often required.

questions.stem_markdown: A previously well unimmunised 3-year-old is seen within 72 hours of close exposure to another child who has developed chickenpox. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation_markdown: The uploaded Term I material gives this post-exposure varicella scenario and identifies immunisation as the best management for a healthy, unimmunised child over 12 months. This distinguishes routine post-exposure vaccination from situations requiring VZIG.

why_others_wrong.A: VZIG is used for selected higher-risk contacts, not the healthy unimmunised child described in the source question.
why_others_wrong.B: Oral acyclovir is not the best answer given in the uploaded source for this scenario.
why_others_wrong.C: IV acyclovir is reserved for more severe or high-risk settings, not this source vignette.
why_others_wrong.E: Supportive care alone does not address the preventive opportunity in the exposed unimmunised child.

key_takeaways: Varicella exposure questions often hinge on host risk category.
Healthy unimmunised children may be managed with post-exposure vaccination.
The uploaded material differentiates vaccination from VZIG use.

questions.stem_markdown: An infant is found to have retinal or subretinal haemorrhages on assessment. What is the most concerning diagnosis suggested by the uploaded source material?
questions.explanation_markdown: Two separate uploaded sources link retinal/subretinal haemorrhages with non-accidental injury, specifically shaken baby syndrome. This makes child abuse the most concerning and best-supported diagnosis.

why_others_wrong.A: This is not the association highlighted in the uploaded question material.
why_others_wrong.B: Although retinal haemorrhages can have other causes, the source set explicitly directs this finding toward NAI.
why_others_wrong.D: Migraine does not explain this examination finding in an infant.
why_others_wrong.E: Vitamin D deficiency is unrelated to retinal haemorrhages in the uploaded material.

key_takeaways: Retinal haemorrhages are a high-stakes child protection clue in the source set.
The uploaded material explicitly links this to shaken baby syndrome.
Child protection diagnoses should be considered promptly when red-flag findings are present.
